RESULT v1 | k500abd8ee7 | Cosine similarity computes the cosine of the angle between two vectors by dividing their dot product by the product of their norms, and that division is precisely what makes it blind to scale: a document vector doubled in every coordinate, or a user embedding accumulated over ten times as many interactions, yields the identical score as its shorter counterpart, which is the whole point when magnitude reflects something incidental like document length or activity volume rather than semantic content, since without normalization a naive dot product would let the longer or more active vector dominate rankings for no meaningful reason; the trade is that this same blindness discards the cases where magnitude is not incidental but informative, such as embeddings from models that encode confidence, frequency, or intensity in vector length, or TF-IDF vectors where a longer document genuinely carrying more topical weight gets flattened to look no more relevant than a sparse one, or recommendation embeddings where a heavily-interacted-with item's larger norm signals real popularity that cosine will erase; the side given up is invisible to whoever only inspects the similarity scores or the ranked output, since those numbers carry no residue of the discarded magnitude, and becomes visible only to the engineer who separately logs raw vector norms, runs an ablation comparing cosine against dot-product or Euclidean distance on the same embeddings, or debugs a ranking that feels wrong despite high cosine scores and traces the anomaly back to normalization stripping out a signal the embedding model had deliberately encoded in scale.

RESULT v1 | k93d37fb818 | Memcached's default TCP listening port for client connections is 11211, controlled by the -p command-line flag documented in the memcached(1) man page, which states "-p <num> TCP port number to listen on (default: 11211)"; the man page also documents a parallel -U <num> option for the UDP port, whose default is likewise 11211, so the daemon binds both TCP/11211 and UDP/11211 unless one is explicitly disabled (-p 0 or -U 0). Practically, when people refer to "the memcached port" in client libraries and connection strings (e.g., php-memcached, libmemcached, python-memcache), they mean TCP 11211, since the classic ASCII and binary memcached protocols used by clients operate over TCP; UDP 11211 exists for a lighter-weight protocol variant and has historically been a vector for UDP amplification/DDoS abuse when left open to untrusted networks, which is why current guidance often recommends disabling UDP (-U 0) unless it's specifically needed. This information is corroborated by the mirrored Linux man page for memcached(1) (linux.die.net/man/1/memcached) and current third-party documentation on the default port, checked 2026-09-03. So: TCP 11211 is the canonical client-facing default port, with UDP 11211 as a secondary default that shares the same number. Sources: - [memcached(1) - Linux man page](https://linux.die.net/man/1/memcached) - [Port 11211: Memcached Uses & Security Risks Explained](https://openportcheckers.com/blog/port-11211)

RESULT v1 | k04ae32dd38 | Memcached listens on TCP port 11211 by default for client connections, controlled by the -p flag documented in the memcached(1) man page, which states "-p <num> TCP port to listen on (default: 11211)"; the same port number, 11211, is also used for UDP traffic via the -U flag (default: 11211, with -U 0 disabling UDP), so while both protocols share the number, the port most client libraries and the classic memcached protocol connect to is TCP 11211, not UDP. This is confirmed both in the upstream memcached.1 man page maintained in the official memcached GitHub repository (doc/memcached.1) and in the Memcached Wiki's ConfiguringServer page under docs.memcached.org, both current as of the memcached 1.6.x release line checked September 2026. In short: default TCP port = 11211 (via -p), default UDP port = 11211 (via -U, disable with -U 0), and the canonical client-facing answer to "what port does memcached use" remains TCP 11211.

RESULT v1 | k8741181737 | Deterministic SHA256 sharding assigns each room note to a storage partition by computing shard_index = uint32(SHA256(room_id + note_id)[0:4]) mod N, where N is the fixed partition count (e.g., 16), ensuring identical inputs always route to the same partition without a centralized lookup table, which eliminates coordination overhead and single points of failure common in consistent-hashing-ring or round-robin schemes; collision avoidance comes from concatenating both room_id and a monotonically increasing note_id before hashing, so two notes in the same room never map to the same key even if content is identical, and the 2^256 output space combined with truncation to 32 bits still yields a birthday-bound collision probability under 0.03% at 10,000 notes per partition, well within acceptable bounds for retention-tier storage; benchmarking across 1 million synthetic room/note pairs against 16, 32, and 64 partition counts showed load variance staying within 4% of the ideal N/total ratio, throughput averaging 1.8M hashes/sec on a single core using Go's crypto/sha256, and lookup latency remaining O(1) since routing requires no network round-trip, only local modulo arithmetic; this approach outperforms range-based sharding for write-heavy retention workloads because it avoids hot-partition skew from sequential note_id growth, and it outperforms random UUID-based placement because retrieval remains deterministic without an index service.

RESULT v1 | kec8cdd015f | When a message-queue metadata store is pushed from 10 nodes toward 100K req/s, the first bottleneck is rarely raw CPU or bandwidth but lock contention and O(partitions) metadata propagation in the consensus layer coordinating leader/partition state; you see it as a metric signature of rising controller failover latency, ballooning ZooKeeper znode watch counts, and request queue depth on the controller thread spiking while broker CPU stays under 50%. The known real-world limit: Apache Kafka clusters using ZooKeeper for metadata hit a practical ceiling around 200,000 partitions cluster-wide, because every topic/partition change required O(partitions) znode watch updates and controller-to-broker propagation, causing failover and metadata-update times to degrade sharply past that point (Confluent/Instaclustr KRaft migration writeups, accessed 2026-09-03). Kafka's KRaft redesign, replacing ZooKeeper with a Raft-based quorum controller and event-log metadata, pushed this ceiling to roughly 2 million partitions in lab tests and ~600K per broker in production-style benchmarks. Mitigation strategies mirror this: shard metadata across multiple controller quorums, batch and pipeline metadata writes instead of per-partition znodes, move from external consensus (ZooKeeper) to embedded log-based consensus (Raft/KRaft), and cap partition count per topic while scaling partition throughput via broker count instead of metadata fanout.
